newsitem.title: GERMANY: ATHLETICS-IAAF TO PAY OUT $11 MILLION PRIZE MONEY IN 1997.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-IAAF TO PAY OUT $11 MILLION PRIZE MONEY IN 1997.

text.p: BONN, Jan 14 (Retuer) - Michael Johnson will pick up $220,000 at this year's world athletics championships, where prize money is to be paid for the first time, if he can repeat his record-breaking double at the Atlanta Olympics.
The International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) gave details on Tuesday of the $11 million it plans to hand out in prize money during 1997.
The figures, due to be announced shortly, include $7.785 million for major championships including the world outdoor championships in Athens and the world indoor championships in Paris.

At the last two world outdoor championships, winners were given a luxury Mercedes car. The gold medallists in Athens will be guaranteed $60,000 in cash with $30,000 and $20,000 for second and third-placed athletes.
World records in Athens will also be worth an extra $100,000. Johnson's historic 200 and 400 triumph in Atlanta included a world record in the shorter event.
The prize money on offer at the less prestigious indoor championships is also competitive with $50,000 for gold medallists and $20,000 and $10,000 for silver and bronze medallists respectively.
The same prize money will be available at the World Cup, which has been struggling in recent years to attract all the top athletes.
A gold medal at the cross-country world championships and the world half-marathon championships will be worth $40,000.
The cash is in addition to the prize money for the grand prix final which will remain at around $3.4 million, officials said.

With big money being paid out in the now established Golden Four series of grand prix meetings in Oslo, Zurich, Brussels and Berlin, the IAAF is keen to make sure its championships are still attractive to the sport's top names.
The IAAF announced last month it planned to pay out prize money for the first time this year but did not give any details of the total amounts at stake.
The sport's governing body plans to pay out almost $20 million at major championships in the next three seasons.
